item.title: @benitoz：投资者探讨黄仁勋去留对英伟达投资逻辑的影响及Jensen回归后的最新动态
item.description:
Peter Lynch said to know what you own and why you own it. Easy advice when $NVDA is ripping. A hell of a lot harder on a Friday at $125 when you don’t know if Jensen is coming back.

I bought my first shares in 2016. I’ve spent a decade studying this company, from the data center floor all the way up to the Nemotron models. I held. I added on the dips. But these last two weeks forced me to answer the same question CNBC asked me on air: What happens to NVIDIA without Jensen?

My answer was pretty blunt. He’s the lifeblood of this company. Customers plan multibillion-dollar data centers around the roadmap he lays out. Engineers who’ve spent their careers working for him have to deliver on it. If you think you can swap out the guy who built those relationships over 33 years and leave every assumption in your spreadsheet untouched, good luck with that.

So yes, if Jensen was out for good, the investment story changed for me. That’s why I pushed the Stand With Jensen petition, went on CNBC and wrote directly to NVIDIA’s board members. I wanted him back, and I told them exactly why.

Then I watched him walk back into NVIDIA. His employees were cheering. He thanked them for a second chance and told them he’d be a better CEO the second time around. After 33 years, the guy still thinks he can get better. That’s the Jensen I bet on.

Last week I was on CNBC being asked what NVIDIA looks like without him. Next week I’ll be at GTC DC hearing from Jensen himself about what he’s building next.

I fought for his comeback. Here we are. See you in DC, Jensen.

item.title: @convequity：分析对比谷歌核电协议与SpaceX天然气轮机成本，指出天然气发电建设成本及速度优势
item.description:
Google's nuclear deal costs about $4.8B per GW to build. We estimate SpaceX's gas turbines at about $0.8B per GW

Constellation is spending more than $4.3B to raise the output of 11 reactors it already runs by 890 MW, and will sell that power to Google ($GOOGL) for 20 years. That is about $4.8B per GW, paid once by Constellation. Google's price is private. At the $85–115 per MWh analysts estimate for similar contracts, we estimate its bill at $0.7–0.9B per GW a year.

The first of the 890 MW is due by 2028 and the last before the end of 2032. The three big nuclear deals signed this year in PJM, the largest US power market, total 6,889 MW. Only 1,513 MW of that is new capacity.

SpaceX ($SPCX) runs its Colossus data centres largely on on-site gas turbines. A joint venture between Solaris and an xAI affiliate is buying about 900 MW of them. Its loan terms imply about $0.7B of spending, or about $0.8B per GW for generators and emissions controls, before fuel. A complete new gas plant costs about $2.4B per GW.

SpaceX is also faster. It ended September with 1.7 GW of compute capacity and expects 2.5–3 GW by the end of December. That is 0.8–1.3 GW added in one quarter, against 0.89 GW from the reactor upgrades for Google by 2032.

Our view: Google's new nuclear power costs two to six times more to build than gas power like SpaceX's and arrives years later. Gas has a fuel bill that nuclear largely avoids, so the gap is in building cost and speed. Our SpaceX report projects about $0.7B per GW to launch and power compute in orbit, if Starship reaches full reuse.

item.title: @convequity：旭创科技透露关键客户已提前给出2028年光模块强劲需求指引，1.6T产品批量出货
item.description:
InnoLight's customers are already giving 2028 demand guidance

InnoLight makes the optical transceivers that carry data between AI servers and switches inside data centres. This month it said some key customers have already given clear demand guidance for 2028.

What InnoLight has disclosed, in date order:
• 27 Apr: customers had given demand guidance for 2026 and 2027, and some key customers were planning their 2028 demand.
• 3 Nov, investor-relations record: the vast majority of 2027 orders already cover the full year.
• Same record: at least one key customer has given clear 2028 demand guidance, and that demand is strong. Guidance from other customers is still being collected.
• Same record: most customers have not cut demand or orders, and some have raised their demand for 1.6T modules, the fastest generation now shipping in volume. InnoLight published the record to answer rumours of overseas order cuts.
• 6 Nov, company announcement: major customers' orders largely cover all of 2027, and some key customers have given clear 2028 guidance.
• 18 Nov: to secure key materials, InnoLight is stocking early, signing long-term supply agreements and prepaying suppliers.
• First nine months of 2026: revenue of RMB 69.5 billion, up 178% on a year earlier, and net profit of RMB 22.2 billion, up 212%.

The 2028 guidance has come unusually early. Customers normally give a supplier next year's demand around the middle of the current year. On that schedule, 2028 guidance would arrive in mid-2027. InnoLight has it in November 2026, about half a year early.

Eoptolink, another large Chinese module maker, points the same way. In an 18 Nov announcement it said customer demand guidance is clear, orders in hand are ample, and it sees no downward revisions or order cuts.

A customer that guides this far ahead is, in our view, trying to secure supply. InnoLight said on 3 Nov that module supply is still tight. We read the 2028 guidance as evidence that demand for AI optics is strong and still building into 2027 and 2028.

The limit: guidance is not a firm order. InnoLight has not named the customers or given volumes. The check is whether the 2028 guidance turns into orders by mid-2027.

Memory prices rose more than fivefold in a year. Foundries are asking for 10% to more than 20% in 2027, and we think they have more room left.

Taiwanese chip designers have received foundry price notices of 10% to more than 20% for the first quarter of 2027. TSMC's own rise is smaller: 3% to 6% on wafers from January, highest on 2nm and 3nm.

Memory moved on a different scale. A 16Gb DDR5 chip cost about $8.70 on contract in October 2025 and $48 in September 2026, according to Team Group's CEO. That is 5.5 times in 11 months. Intel's CEO said in September that memory prices "have gone up five, six, and seven times". Counterpoint puts third-quarter DRAM revenue near $200 billion, close to five times a year earlier.

We think the slower pace helps the foundries. A chip buyer that has paid five times more for memory can pay 10% more for wafers, so foundries can keep raising prices in steps. Their revenue and profit should also be steadier. Part of memory is already turning down: TrendForce expects NAND flash contract prices to be flat to 5% lower in the first quarter of 2027.

The second-tier foundries are where the price rises spread next. They make older-generation chips and had spare capacity earlier this year. Most of it is now in use. UMC ($UMC) ran at 85% of capacity in the second quarter and 92% in the third. GlobalFoundries ($GFS) is in the high 80s, Vanguard is at about 90% and SMIC at 97%.

Their prices are following. UMC expects its average selling price to rise about 10% in 2027 and says shipment growth will be limited by capacity. GlobalFoundries reported its first year-on-year price rise since 2023 in the third quarter and expects about a 10% lift from price and product mix in 2027. Powerchip is negotiating rises of 10% to 20%.

A 10% rise is large for these companies. UMC's gross margin is 34%. If its costs stayed flat, a 10% price rise would lift that to about 40%. UMC says part of the rise covers its own higher costs, so the real gain will be smaller.

The risk is spare capacity coming back. GlobalFoundries went more than two years without a year-on-year price rise before the third quarter. Second-tier price rises last only while these fabs stay close to full.

item.title: @convequity：分析认为3D DRAM芯片设计面临散热与可靠性结构性限制，代工厂与制造集成成关键
item.description:
For investors looking at 3D DRAM chip designers such as d-Matrix and Fractile, the hard problems left are heat and reliability, and the company that designs the chip does not control the fix. We think that puts a structural ceiling on how far a fabless designer like Fractile can set its 3D DRAM apart.

d-Matrix has shown publicly how a designer can work around the heat. Fractile, a private fabless startup working on 3D DRAM, has not shown comparable work publicly.

3D DRAM means stacking memory directly on the compute chip. The connections between the two layers are mostly solved. Heat and reliability are not.

DRAM loses its data faster as it gets hotter. As temperature rises, each cell holds its data for a shorter time, so the memory has to be refreshed more often, and error rates climb.

A high-power logic die is the hottest part of the system. Put DRAM on it and the memory sits in the worst thermal spot there is. Heat from compute has to pass through the memory stack, or around it, to reach the cooler.

The fixes are process and packaging work: bonding materials, thermal paths, DRAM cells built for high temperatures, and test and yield at the level of the whole stack. That work belongs to the foundry and the memory maker.

A fabless designer, a company that designs chips and has someone else manufacture them, can do less. It can keep hot compute blocks away from sensitive memory banks, throttle, add error correction, or refresh more aggressively. These steps work around the physics, but a designer cannot change it.

d-Matrix is the reference case. It flips the stack and puts the compute die on top of the DRAM, so the cold plate sits directly on the hottest silicon and heat does not have to pass through the memory. That is useful engineering.

The other route is vertical integration. Huawei controls or tightly couples process, packaging and design, so it can tune the memory cell, the bond and the logic floorplan together. A fabless startup cannot.

That is why we see the ceiling as structural, and it limits what differentiation can mean for a company like Fractile. What we watch is whether Fractile shows public thermal and reliability work comparable to what d-Matrix has shown.

item.title: @convequity：AI内存需求转向速度：HBM堆叠层数增加如何影响数据传输与处理器性能
item.description:
For investors in AI memory: demand is moving toward speed, and a taller HBM stack only adds capacity. AI inference that answers quickly now commands a premium, and the memory speed it depends on is set by the stack's external interface.

An HBM stack is several layers of DRAM memory on a base die. The base die is a logic die that handles input and output, control and everything else that is not storage. In a conventional package, the base die talks to the processor through a silicon interposer.

Think of that package as a residential tower next to a one-storey office where the residents work. The HBM stack is the tower, the processor is the office, and the interposer is an underground passage between them.

To get to work, residents ride the elevators down. The elevators are TSVs, the vertical connections that run down through the stacked memory dies. There are about 12,000 of them across a 12-high stack.

At the bottom, the residents squeeze through a few exit gates, which are the stack's 2,048 pins, and then cross the passage.

Adding floors houses more residents, but they all still leave through the same few gates. Stacking more memory dies works the same way. Capacity goes up, and the external interface's width and signalling speed decide how much data reaches the processor.

Stack the memory directly above the logic and the residents live above their workplace. Elevators spread across the building drop them right next to the desks they need, with no shared exit and no trip next door.

In silicon, dense vertical connections give many more parallel paths between memory and logic over shorter wires. That also cuts the energy spent moving data.

Our view is that a taller HBM stack should be read as more capacity, and that the interface is where to look for how fast data reaches the processor.

item.title: @convequity：郭明錤称谷歌削减2027年博通TPU订单，市场反应与潜在影响分析
item.description:
Ming-Chi Kuo says Google cut 1 million Broadcom TPUs for 2027. I doubt those chips go unsold.

Kuo's 20 November supply-chain survey says Google cut 2027 shipments of the Broadcom-designed TPU 8i by about 1 million units, roughly 20%, mostly the higher-priced 8i Max, and will take more of MediaTek's TPU 8t. Broadcom ($AVGO) fell about 12% that day and lost about $200 billion of market value, in a session when the whole chip sector sold off. Neither company has commented.

I would treat the check with caution. Supply-chain checks from Taiwan tend to favor Taiwanese vendors, and checks on the US side tend to favor US vendors. The truth usually sits between the two.

Suppose the cut is real. At about $5,500–6,000 per TPU 8i, a price from a single expert call, 1 million units is about $5.5–6 billion of 2027 revenue. The 8i Max costs more, so the true figure would be higher. The market value lost that day was still more than 30 times that revenue.

The capacity would not sit idle either. AI chips are still short, and Kuo's own post cites a tight supply chain. Broadcom's CEO Hock Tan said in September that Broadcom expects Anthropic to deploy 5 GW of TPU 8i in 2027, meaning 5 gigawatts of data center power filled with these chips, with another 10 GW in view for 2028. Kuo's 16 November note put about 14 million Broadcom-designed 8i units with Anthropic across 2028 and 2029. If Google takes fewer chips, Broadcom has wafers and packaging slots to give to customers already waiting.

I also find Kuo's reason hard to follow. He says frontier model development gets first call on Google's compute. A growing part of that development is reinforcement learning after the main training run, where the model produces large volumes of output and is graded on it. That is inference work, the job the 8i was built for.

The risk is power. If Anthropic and other buyers cannot get data center power in 2027, the freed chips slip into 2028. Even so, I read the selloff as a better chance to buy Broadcom than a reason to sell it.

item.title: @convequity：微软选择英特尔EMIB先进封装用于Azure芯片，英特尔代工业务实现重要突破
item.description:
Intel's foundry turnaround is starting in packaging, and Microsoft just signed up

$MSFT said on 18 November that it will use Intel Foundry's EMIB packaging for Azure's own chips. It is the first company to announce that publicly.

We read the chip as the next Maia AI accelerator. TechPowerUp reports that next-generation Maia and Cobalt will be packaged at $INTC. Maia 200 is packaged today on $TSM's CoWoS, where $NVDA gets priority on capacity.

An AI accelerator is several chips in one package: a compute die plus stacks of high-bandwidth memory. CoWoS mounts all of them on one large piece of silicon. EMIB keeps the cheaper standard package base and embeds small silicon bridges only where two chips connect. EMIB is in the low hundreds of dollars per chip, against roughly $900–1,000 for CoWoS on a Rubin-class accelerator.

The release says EMIB. We think the version is EMIB-T. EMIB-T adds vertical connections through the bridge, so power reaches the chips from directly underneath. Large AI chips with many memory stacks need that.

Google is reportedly making the same move. Part of TPU v9 will switch from CoWoS to EMIB-T. Some sources also say MediaTek and Meta will adopt EMIB too.

On who designs future Maia chips: Marvell and Global Unichip reportedly do that work today. The Information reported Microsoft was in talks to move it to $AVGO. We see Broadcom as the front runner, and a Broadcom-designed Maia on EMIB-T would put a second major custom AI chip family on Intel's packaging.

The limit is yield. TrendForce put EMIB-T substrate yield near 35% in Q3, against a 50% year-end target. But given how much momentum EMIB is getting now and Intel's continued dogfooding via using EMIB for its own products, I think they will eventually get it done especially if they are wiling to lower the spec.

item.title: @convequity：特斯拉发布Powercore可将34.5kV电网电力一步转换至800V直流电
item.description:
Tesla's Powercore takes 34.5 kV grid power to 800V DC in one step at 7.4 MW. This is a huge deal for the 800V HVDC landscape.

$TSLA unveiled Powercore on 17 November. One cabinet takes 10 to 34.5 kV AC and puts out 800 to 2,000 V DC, with 98.86% peak efficiency and first units operating in 2027. Tesla is working with $NVDA to certify it for 800V DC data centers.

This changes part of what we wrote in June, when we argued 800V DC was not ready for mainstream adoption. Our reason was the conversion path. Solid-state transformers in production worked at low voltage only. A data center had to step the grid's 13 to 20 kV down to about 400V AC, convert that to 800V DC, then step down again to 50V for the servers. We put the direct path from the grid to 800V at two or more years away.

Think of voltage as water pressure. The transmission line is the trunk main. The substation transformer drops it to a 34.5 kV district main. The path we described in June uses two sets of valves to get from the district main to the 800V pipe that feeds the server racks. Powercore uses one.

Most Powercore users, including SpaceX ($SPCX), will pair it with behind-the-meter natural gas turbines coupled with Megapack. The last drop inside the rack, from 800V to about 50V and then 12V, is not part of what Tesla announced. Powercore stops at 800V, so the 50V step we flagged in June is still there.

So Tesla is addressing the main gap we flagged in June, with a product that first operates in 2027 and that Nvidia has not yet certified.

How does Tesla do it? No silicon carbide (SiC) transistor in volume production blocks 12 kV or more on its own. $WOLF has shown a 10 kV device, and it is not in volume supply. Converters in this class stack many cells in series, each built on 1.2 to 3.3 kV SiC parts, so the cells share the grid voltage between them. Tesla has not published Powercore's circuit design, switch material or supplier. Our reading is stacked SiC cells, because gallium nitride (GaN) in production is mostly rated 650V and below.

Tesla builds its converters in-house, about 3 terawatts so far, and says Powercore uses "U.S. and imported parts". It does not own a SiC fab. Teardowns of Model 3 and Model Y inverters show SiC chips from $STM, and $ON is reportedly a second source for the cars.

Tesla is ahead on size, and it has company. Amperesand said it would ship 30 MW of one-step 800V units in 2026, built on Wolfspeed 3.3 kV modules. Delta Electronics (http://2308.TW) has had a unit running at a Chinese data center since February. Heron Power, founded by former Tesla executive Drew Baglino, plans volume production of a 4.2 MW data-center unit in late 2027. $ETN has a 2 MW, 15 kV unit that passed a new UL standard, and Infineon (http://IFX.DE) supplies SiC for Eaton's platform. Tesla's edge is 7.4 MW per cabinet, converter manufacturing at scale, and Megapack batteries on the same DC bus.

The read-across by layer:

1) Medium-voltage gear. Powercore replaces the conventional transformer, switchgear and rectifier between the substation and the rack. $VRT and Schneider Electric (http://SU.PA) sell that equipment and, per an industry survey, have not announced a commercial solid-state transformer. JPMorgan reportedly says Powercore would compete with traditional data-center electrical suppliers once it ships.

2) SiC chips. Every one-step converter needs a large number of SiC switches, whoever builds the cabinet. Chinese industry estimates put this demand at roughly $500M a year by 2030. If Tesla takes share, more of that volume goes to whichever supplier Tesla picks.

3) Rack power. The 800V to 50V step stays with the chip vendors Nvidia has named for 800V: Infineon, STMicro, ON, $NVTS and InnoScience (http://2577.HK). Navitas and InnoScience sell GaN for that step, which Powercore does not touch. Wolfspeed is not on Nvidia's list. It would also be worth tracking whether Tesla expands into this layer itself.

item.title: @convequity：Keysight第四财季订单达23.4亿美元，显示客户持续采购1.6T光链路设备
item.description:
Keysight's orders show customers are still paying for 1.6T optical links

Optics shares have fallen this month. Innolight lost 9% in one session on 6 November and Applied Optoelectronics is down 45% in a month. Keysight ($KEYS) took $2.34 billion of orders in fiscal Q4 against $1.99 billion of revenue, 1.17 times. AI bookings for the full year were about 2.5 times the prior year's, and the number of AI customers nearly doubled.

Keysight makes the test instruments that prove a high-speed link works, and a transceiver maker buys from it twice. In R&D, engineers use its bit-error-rate testers and lab oscilloscopes to design and qualify each new module speed. On the production line, its digital communication analyzers, sampling oscilloscopes that measure a module's optical signal, test 800G and 1.6T modules before they ship. In August management put its data center link business at about two-thirds R&D and one-third manufacturing, with the mix moving toward production as 1.6T ramps. The other buyers sit on either side of the module: chip designers validating silicon before tape-out, switch and cable makers qualifying 1.6T copper and optical links, and cloud companies emulating AI traffic on a cluster's network before deployment. A separate business sells wafer test systems to foundries and memory makers, where orders grew double digits on advanced nodes, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and silicon photonics. Foundries are now taking silicon photonics into commercial production, which adds optical test to the electrical wafer test Keysight already sells. Management expects the bigger step-up from co-packaged optics (CPO), which moves the optics into the switch package, in 2028.

Customers buy much of this equipment when they develop and qualify the next link speed, before modules ship in volume, so Keysight's orders move ahead of the optics makers' revenue. Management said 1.6T is early in its ramp and 3.2T is already in R&D. Our estimate: the CFO guided Q1 orders down by a mid-single-digit percentage, which puts them near $2.2 billion against a $2.05 billion revenue guide, about 1.08 times. Risk: the CFO said $200–300 million of the backlog built up because Keysight could not ship fast enough, so that part measures its own supply shortage.

item.title: @convequity：Palo Alto Networks将以45亿美元股票收购Applied Compute以训练安全模型
item.description:
Palo Alto Networks is buying the tooling to train its own security models

$PANW agreed on 18 November to pay $4.5B in stock for Applied Compute, founded in 2025 by three former OpenAI researchers. Most coverage treats it as an expensive research hire. We see PANW moving from securing other companies' AI to training security into the model itself.

Enterprises have long treated security and utility as a trade-off. Tighter security made software harder to use, so buyers chose utility and underinvested in security. AI changes that choice. A company will only let an agent act on its data once it trusts the model, so wide AI adoption needs security built into the model.

Applied Compute post-trains open-weight models, which means it takes a published model and trains it further on one customer's data for one job, mostly with reinforcement learning. It then serves the tuned model on its own cloud, and the customer keeps the weights.

Fireworks, Baseten and Together sell much the same thing. All three offer fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on open-weight models, and all three say the customer keeps the weights. Fireworks launched reinforcement fine-tuning in June 2025. Baseten made its reinforcement learning toolkit generally available on 6 November. So post-training is not what sets Applied Compute apart. It leans harder on researchers who sit with the customer and build the training environments from that company's own data. Arora said no other team matched its pedigree in post-training open-weight models. We think the edge is the team more than the product.

PANW did not buy the largest open-model host. Fireworks was reportedly valued near $17.5B. PANW paid 38% above the $3.25B round Applied Compute closed on 2 November, and about 45x on our arithmetic: $4.5B against ARR that topped $100M. Nikesh Arora told investors PANW looked at nine providers first. We think PANW bought a good asset at a price it could afford, and the return depends on how Arora builds it inside PANW.

The baseline case is that PANW trains its own security models. Arora said it will train more than 35 specialized security use cases. PANW holds years of attack data from its firewalls and Cortex, and Applied Compute supplies the tooling to turn that data into weights PANW owns. Our SaaS Survival Scorecard counts that step under Model-Layer Leverage. Google and Microsoft have trained security models and, in our view, neither has shown a breakthrough. PANW has the stronger data for this job.

The larger opportunity is making Chinese open-weight models safe for enterprises to use. Applied Compute's inference page lists Kimi, GLM, Qwen, DeepSeek and MiniMax next to Nvidia's Nemotron. The strongest open-weight models today are mostly Chinese, and PANW has not named which it will train on. If PANW can post-train a Chinese model for security work and show customers it is safe to deploy, enterprises can use the best open models without settling for weaker Western ones. Arora told investors this business could grow larger than PANW's cybersecurity business, and PANW expects more than $1B of ARR from the deal by fiscal 2029.

A third path is competing with Fireworks and Baseten for general open-model customers. Our confidence in that one is low.

We are surprised PANW moved this late. But enterprise AI adoption is still early, so the timing still works. The deal closes in PANW's fiscal Q3 2027, and no security model trained on Applied Compute's tooling has shipped yet.

item.description:
Alibaba's 50% cloud rebound is now a bet on its own chips

$BABA told investors the new US export rule will cost it cloud growth next year. The bigger story is what CEO Wu Yongming says will replace the lost compute.

The rule took effect on Nov 19, the day of the call. It restricts chip exports to overseas data centers that supply large volumes of compute to Chinese companies, on top of the existing limits on buying advanced chips. Both outside routes to compute narrow at once.

Wu says the rules will affect next year's products and services. Cloud revenue grew 53% last quarter. The preliminary target for fiscal 2028 (April 2027 to March 2028) is 30–45%, and Wu says the long-term 20 GW data center target may be revised down.

Then the roadmap for T-Head, Alibaba's in-house chip unit, all per the call:

• Zhenwu M890: fully rolled out this year
• V900: 3x the M890's computing performance, mass production in Q1 2027
• V900 super-node clusters: commercial scale in Q2 2027
• J900: large-scale production in 2028

A super-node is many chips networked tightly enough to work as one large machine, which is what training a big model needs.

Wu says that after 2027 most of the new AI chip capacity Alibaba adds will be its own chips, with other domestic chips bought mainly for inference. He says Qwen is already training its next-generation model on T-Head chips.

The promised payoff is cloud growth back to 50% or higher in calendar 2028.

I read that 50% as conditional. Wu says the market is still supply constrained, so growth depends on how much compute Alibaba can deploy. That makes the 2028 number a bet on the V900 ramping on schedule. If mass production slips, the rebound slips with it.

The call gave no V900 yields, no comparison with Nvidia, and no evidence of training on large V900 clusters. The same US rule also tightens foreign foundry access for chip designers in restricted countries, which has forced many tier 2 Chinese AI chip makers to scramble for domestic process node capacity out of Samsung and TSMC.

The risk has not gone away. It has moved from Washington's export list to T-Head's supply chain.

item.title: @convequity：DeepSeek完成新一轮约15亿美元融资，估值达87亿美元并持续扩大昇腾芯片集群
item.description:
DeepSeek at about $87 billion is still cheap for what it owns

Caixin reports DeepSeek has closed a second round of about 100 billion yuan ($15 billion) for about 17.3% of the company. That works out to about 578 billion yuan, roughly $87 billion, up about 65% from the 350 billion yuan of the July round. I thought July was too low, and I think this price still undervalues DeepSeek's models and know-how against its Western peers. Anthropic ($ANT) closed its first trading day at $1.27 trillion and $1.6T on diluted basis, about 15 times more. I understand the discount. DeepSeek has always put research ahead of selling its models, and its consumer app is free.

Why raise now? Chips first. In an investor call that leaked in July, founder Liang Wenfeng said DeepSeek had about 16,000 Huawei Ascend 950 cards while the big internet companies got more than 100,000. Then Beijing noticed this and helped Deepsee in pushing Huawei for priority, and by September Bloomberg reported an order for at least 160,000 Ascend 950DT chips for a cluster in Inner Mongolia. That order is reported at about $2.56 billion, about $16,000 a chip. At that price $15 billion pays for more than 900,000 chips, and Huawei's 2026 output of this chip is estimated at 200,000 to 300,000. I expect most of the money to go into bigger clusters in China. Power and construction are fast there, so the pace depends on how many chips Huawei can deliver.

Demand is the second reason. DeepSeek's status page shows eight incidents since October, including an outage of nearly five hours on 15 October. On 16 November it capped daily use of its free app for the first time, with a notice citing a compute shortage. DeepSeek wanted to stay a research-first company, and it is raising $15 billion because usage has grown faster than its compute.

item.title: @convequity：台积电据报针对自定义芯片客户设立信用额度并要求现金预付，博通等资金充裕企业具优势
item.description:
TSMC's reported credit screen favors Broadcom over smaller custom-chip designers

Commercial Times reports that TSMC ($TSM) now sets a credit limit for each customer from its balance sheet. Orders above the limit are paid in cash, and some customers prepay to reserve capacity. A widely shared X post and India Today's headline read it as TSMC reacting to Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia ($NVDA). The reports say the rule mainly applies to custom AI chip designers. TSMC has not commented and the report names no customer.

The reason is timing. A custom-chip designer pays TSMC when the wafers are made and collects from its own customer only when finished chips ship, after packaging. AI orders keep getting larger, so TSMC carries more risk on each customer and asks for the cash first.

Broadcom ($AVGO), which designs Google's TPU chips with Google, made $13.7B of free cash flow in its August quarter and holds $24B of cash. Alchip, a Taiwanese custom-chip designer, raised $510M overseas in June. Our estimate: $13.7B over 91 days is about $150M a day, so Alchip's raise equals about 3.4 days of Broadcom's free cash flow. Marvell ($MRVL) is prepaying about $1B to key suppliers this fiscal year, about twice what Alchip raised.

Lenders are tightening in the same way. Those funding Nvidia's $500B GPU financing platform reportedly want more than the 25% guarantee Nvidia offered.

If TSMC gives capacity to customers that pay first, Broadcom and Nvidia keep their leading-edge wafers, and designers that fund orders by raising outside money lose slots first. A cloud company choosing a design partner needs that partner to get wafers, so we expect more custom-chip programs to go to Broadcom.

item.description:
回复 @convequity
Broadcom's shared backend across many custom chip programs is a strength, and we think Broadcom could build 3D DRAM if a hyperscaler asked for it.

Fractile is a private company betting on 3D DRAM, which is memory stacked directly on the compute chip. The question venture investors and non-specialists probably ask most is why a custom-ASIC house like Broadcom, which designs chips to order for individual customers, would not build this instead.

Fractile's CEO, Walter Goodwin, answered that Broadcom runs one shared backend platform across many custom ASIC programs, and Fractile does not.

We read that as a fact about business models, and one that favors Broadcom. A shared backend spreads tooling, IP and packaging know-how across many customers, so each new chip program draws on work already done for the others.

On the technology, Broadcom is also pursuing 3D SRAM on logic. That is what TSMC's packaging offers, and every serious designer evaluates it.

We believe Broadcom has looked at 3D DRAM too and has chosen to hold back heavy investment for now because it judges 3D DRAM less mature than 3D SRAM.

What we watch for is a hyperscaler, one of the large cloud companies that order custom chips, asking Broadcom for 3D DRAM. If that request comes, we think Broadcom could deliver it.

item.title: @convequity：分析人工智能负载变化对HBM与SRAM存储芯片市场的影响
item.description:
HBM won the training era because it sits in the middle of a three-rung memory ladder, and agent workloads are now moving demand toward the one closest to the compute, on-die SRAM.

In rough orders of magnitude, each step on the ladder trades about 10x. On-die SRAM costs about 10x what HBM costs per bit, delivers about 10x the bandwidth, and holds about one-tenth the capacity. Conventional off-package DRAM is about 10x cheaper than HBM, with about 10x less bandwidth and about 10x more capacity.

Each rung gives up one resource to gain another. HBM offers a usable balance of cost, bandwidth and capacity, and most AI accelerators use it.

What changed is the workload mix. Agents make many sequential calls. For that pattern, time-to-token, the wait before a response begins, matters more than raw throughput, so low-latency inference now commands a premium.

At the same time, sliding-window attention and similar context techniques cap the KV cache, the working memory a model holds for each conversation. A capped conversation needs less memory capacity.

So capacity demand falls and bandwidth demand rises. SRAM gives up capacity, which buyers now need less of, and supplies bandwidth, which they need more of. That has created a real market for SRAM-heavy inference chips, which were once a niche bet.

The cost gap between HBM and SRAM is also narrowing. Memory prices keep rising, so HBM's cost per gigabyte is creeping toward SRAM's. SRAM is built on TSMC logic nodes, and TSMC has not pushed the kind of aggressive price increases memory makers have. Conventional DRAM is getting more expensive too, because memory makers are shifting production to HBM and leaving less DRAM supply.

We are watching the cost-per-bit gap between HBM and SRAM, which is about 10x and narrowing.

item.title: @convequity：分析指出美国AI大模型订阅制的大幅折扣令中国模型的个人用户价格优势消失
item.description:
Once subscriptions are counted, the best Chinese models can cost an individual user more than the best American ones.

The reason is the flat-fee plan. OpenAI, Google and Anthropic each sell individuals a subscription, and a subscription buys far more usage than the same money spent on the API.

In our examples, OpenAI's plans deliver about 20x the API-equivalent value, and heavy Claude Code use can reach 40x to 100x. For a heavy user, a personal plan can work out to roughly a 97% discount to API prices.

That discount removes China's price advantage with individual users.

Companies buying at scale are in a different position. Those running AI inside their own products and workflows pay by usage through the API, and at API rates Chinese models are still cheaper.

We think the labs do this on purpose. They can burn spare capacity or accept thin consumer margins to win users. Those users then carry the tool into their workplaces, where the enterprise and API money is.

item.title: @GaryMarcus：观点称不能简单将某项特定智力任务的难度类比并推导AI自动化科研的进程
item.description:
so reductive it is stupid 🤦‍♂️

@andrewgwils：Saying RH is harder than AI research and therefore we should expect AI research to be automated soon is also much too reductionistic. It’s like saying beating the world’s grandmaster at chess is harder than being a good surgeon, and so we should expect surgery to be automated once we “figure out the plumbing”.

We would laugh at the idea that a system like deep blue could be adapted to become a good surgeon, nevermind a great scientist, if only we figured out a few details.

Intellectual difficulty is not one dimensional, and there is not necessarily much transfer from one ability to the next, especially when a system has been exhaustively trained to be strong in a highly specialized setting. That’s not to say there won’t be some transfer in this instance, but we know when in people when someone is smart in one way we wouldn’t expect them to be smart in others, and that’s much more the case with these systems than people. It’s not just plumbing.
